questions.q: What does a one-to-one relationship mean between two tables?
options: Each row in Table A corresponds to at most one row in Table B, and vice versa
Every row in Table A must match many rows in Table B
The two tables must have identical column names
Table B can only ever contain one row total
questions.explain: One-to-one caps the match at exactly one row on each side, not many.

questions.q: What column trick enforces a strict one-to-one relationship?
options: Making the same column both the primary key and a foreign key
Adding a UNIQUE constraint to every column in the table
Using an IDENTITY column instead of an INT
Creating two separate primary keys on one table
questions.explain: A primary key can't repeat, so if that same column is also a foreign key, at most one matching row can exist on each side.

questions.q: In AdventureWorks2012, why is HumanResources.Employee to Person.Person a real one-to-one example?
options: Every Employee row has BusinessEntityID as both its own primary key and a foreign key to Person, so each Employee matches exactly one Person
Employee and Person are actually the same physical table
Every Person is automatically an Employee
Employee has no primary key at all
questions.explain: Not every Person is an Employee (customers and vendors are people too), but every Employee row maps to exactly one Person row via that shared key.

questions.q: Why would you split one real-world thing into two one-to-one tables instead of a single table?
options: When one side is optional, holds rarely-used columns, or represents a specific subtype of a more general entity
It's always required by SQL Server for performance reasons
One-to-one relationships cannot exist within a single table under any circumstances
To make joins impossible
questions.explain: A supertype/subtype split (like Person/Employee) is the classic reason to use a one-to-one relationship instead of one big table.

questions.q: Why is one-to-one the rarest of the three relationship shapes?
options: If two things always pair up exactly one-to-one, they're often just combined into a single table instead
SQL Server technically forbids more than a handful of one-to-one relationships per database
One-to-one relationships require a special edition of SQL Server
It's actually the most common relationship shape, not the rarest
questions.explain: Splitting into two tables only makes sense when there's a specific reason — optionality, rarely-used columns, or a subtype pattern.
